title: Osmosis across a semi-permeable membrane

bodies.name: Membrane
bodies.label: Semi-permeable membrane
bodies.describe: Its pores let water molecules through but not the larger solute molecules.

bodies.name: Tagged water molecule
bodies.label: Tagged water molecule
bodies.describe: One water molecule marked so you can follow it, or ride it (POV).

bodies.name: Piston
bodies.label: Piston · extra pressure on the solution
bodies.describe: Pressing on the solution side pushes back against the osmotic flow.

net water flow.label: more water crosses into the solution

lessons.title: Watch the water move
lessons.question: Which way does water move?
lessons.text: The tank starts with both levels equal. Water molecules (blue) cross the membrane pores in both directions; the solute molecules (orange) bounce off it on the right. Wait for the net water flow.
lessons.explain: Solute that cannot enter the pores lowers the chemical potential of the water on its side, so more water enters the solution than leaves it. In real membranes this flow is mostly bulk flow through the pores, driven by a pressure difference set up inside them; it is not water simply "diffusing down its own gradient" (Kramer & Myers 2013). The particle picture here shows the direction and the balance, not the molecular mechanism.
lessons.opens: How does one molecule get across?

lessons.title: Ride one molecule
lessons.question: How does one molecule get across?
lessons.text: You are now riding a single tagged water molecule, jostled by thermal motion. Watch the pink membrane ahead and wait until the molecule slips through a pore.
lessons.explain: No single molecule knows which way is "downhill". It wanders at random, and when it reaches a pore it may pass in either direction. The net flow is a small imbalance between two large, opposite streams. In living cells water crosses mainly through aquaporins, channels that pass water molecules in single file, discovered by Preston et al. (1992).

lessons.title: Equilibrium
lessons.question: When does the flow stop?
lessons.text: Follow the solution level: it rises while the pure-water level falls. The extra height presses back on the membrane. Wait for equilibrium.
lessons.explain: The higher column pushes water back, and the flow stops when its hydrostatic pressure ρgΔh balances the solute's effect: here near 40 mm, where −ln x_w = 2KΔh. For dilute solutions this is van 't Hoff's law, π = cRT (van 't Hoff 1887): the osmotic pressure grows with the number of dissolved particles, not with their kind. In the real world a 0.01 mol/L sugar solution at 25 °C has π ≈ 25 kPa, enough to hold up a column of water 2.5 m high.
lessons.opens: Does more solute make the column taller?

lessons.title: More solute
lessons.question: Does more solute make the column taller?
lessons.text: Double the solute to 90 molecules. The tank refills from equal levels. Watch the solution rise higher this time, and wait for equilibrium.
lessons.explain: With twice the solute the column settles near 65 mm instead of 40 mm. It is not exactly double, because −ln x_w grows a little faster than the solute fraction, and the incoming water dilutes the solution as it rises. In dilute solutions the osmotic pressure is proportional to the solute concentration (π = cRT).
lessons.opens: Can pressure push the water back?

lessons.title: Push back: reverse osmosis
lessons.question: Can pressure push the water back?
lessons.text: Lower the piston onto the solution with 120 mm of water pressure, more than the osmotic pressure. Watch which way the water now crosses.
lessons.explain: Pressure on the solution raises the water's chemical potential there. Once it exceeds the osmotic pressure, the net flow reverses and water is squeezed out of the solution through the membrane, leaving the solute behind. The flow follows J = Lp(ΔP − σΔπ) (Kedem & Katchalsky 1958). Desalination plants work this way: seawater has an osmotic pressure of about 27 bar, so they press it at 55–80 bar.
